verdict.rationale: The word pattern across both Testaments presents God knowing all things completely and eternally. In the Hebrew Bible layer (OSHB, the Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible) the verb 'to know' (yada, Strong H3045, queried at 945 word occurrences over 874 verses, Old Testament only) functions as the qal perfect (the simple active completed-action form of the Hebrew verb) predicate over Psalm 139, where 'there is not a word on my tongue' (eyn millah bilshoni, H0369 plus H4405) denies any word God does not already know. Isaiah 46:10 stacks 'declaring' (maggid, H5046) with the temporal pair 'beginning' (reshit, H7225) and 'end' (acharit, H0319) plus 'my counsel will stand' (etsah taqum, H6098) to declare the end from the beginning. The Greek vocabulary adds 'to know beforehand' (proginosko, G4267), 'to determine beforehand' (proorizo, G4309), 'he knows all things' (ginoskei panta, G1097 plus G3956) in 1 John 3:20, and the absolute negation 'there is no creature hidden' (ouk estin ktisis aphanes, G0852) in Hebrews 4:13. The complicating now-I-know texts use the same qal perfect 'to know' (yada) inside a 'testing' (nasah) frame (Genesis 22:1 with H5254, then Genesis 22:12 with H3045, paired explicitly in Deuteronomy 8:2), so they read as demonstration, not acquisition of new knowledge. The spread across the whole Bible (pan-canonical) is dense, and the verdict is variant robust (stable against textual variants).

scripture.reasoning: YHWH (the LORD) is addressed with 'you have searched me' (chaqartani) and the qal imperfect-consecutive (a Hebrew narrative past form built on the simple active stem) 'and you know me' (wattedaa). The opening line places complete personal knowing as the controlling predicate over the whole psalm. The queried verb 'to know' (yada, H3045) here is the same root that recurs in Psalm 139:2 and 139:4.

'You know my sitting down and my rising up' (yadata shivti uqumi) pairs sitting and rising as a merism (a two-part figure naming the extremes to mean the whole) of total daily action, and 'from afar' (merachoq) adds spatial distance. The queried 'to know' (yada) here is qal perfect 2ms (the simple active completed-action form, second person masculine singular, tagged HVqp2ms), identical in form to the divine heart-knowing of 1 Kings 8:39. The lexical force is that no posture or distance limits the divine knowing.

'You are familiar with all my ways' (wekol derakhay hiskantah) uses 'all' (kol, H3605, the highest-frequency totalizing quantifier, a word meaning 'all' or 'every', in the OSHB layer at over five thousand occurrences) with 'way' (derek) to assert that all my ways are familiar to YHWH (the LORD). The object of the knowing is grammatically total.

'For there is not a word on my tongue, behold, O LORD, you know it altogether' (ki eyn millah bilshoni hen yadata kullah) states that before a word is on the tongue YHWH (the LORD) already knows the whole of it. The existential negator 'there is not' (ayin, H0369) forecloses any prior moment in which the word is unknown to God, so the construction asserts prior knowledge of an unspoken word.

'Such knowledge is too wonderful for me, it is high, I cannot attain it' (peliah daat mimmenni nisgevah) confesses that this knowledge is too wonderful and too high. 'Wonderful' (peliah, H6383) is a near-hapax (a word that occurs only once or twice in the entire Bible), queried at only two occurrences in the canon (here and Judges 13:18, of the angel's wonderful name), so the speaker grades the divine knowing as qualitatively beyond creaturely reach.

'There is no searching of his understanding' (eyn cheqer litvunato) states there is no searching out of his understanding. The noun 'searching' (cheqer, H2714) under the negator 'there is not' (eyn) declares that the divine understanding has no findable limit, the positive counterpart to the creature unable to reach it in Psalm 139:6. Psalm 147:5 echoes this with 'understanding' (tevunah, H8394) plus 'no number' (ein mispar).

'I am God, and there is no other, I am God, and there is none like me' (anoki el we-eyn od we-efes kamoni) places God in an exclusivity claim. The piled negations 'there is not' (eyn, H0369) and 'no one else' (efes, H0657) deny any peer who could rival the knowing asserted in the next verse, so the omniscience (all-knowing) claim is grounded in unique deity.

'Declaring the end from the beginning, and from ancient times what is not yet done' (maggid mereshit acharit umiqqedem asher lo naasu) declares the end from the beginning, and from antiquity what is not yet done. The hiphil participle (the Hebrew causative form, 'to cause to declare') 'declaring' (maggid, from nagad, H5046) with the temporal pair 'beginning' (reshit, H7225) and 'end' (acharit, H0319) asserts present declaration of future events. 'My counsel will stand, and I will accomplish all my desire' (atsati taqum we-kol cheftsi eeseh) adds that the divine counsel (etsah, H6098) stands and every desire is enacted, so prior knowing and prior purpose are joined.

'The LORD knows the thoughts of man' (YHWH yodea machshevot adam) states that the LORD knows the thoughts of man. Queried 'to know' (yada) here is the qal participle (the simple active ongoing-action form, tagged HVqrmsa, masculine singular active), framing the knowing as a standing characteristic, and the object 'thoughts' (machshevot) makes inner cognition the field of divine knowledge.

'For you, you only, know the hearts of all the children of mankind' (attah yadata levadeka eth levav kol bene haadam) confesses that you alone know the heart of all the sons of men. Queried 'to know' (yada) here is qal perfect 2ms (the simple active completed-action form, second person masculine singular, HVqp2ms), the exact morphological form used in Psalm 139:2 and 139:4, which is the positive control showing that the verb form itself carries exhaustive (complete, leaving nothing out) divine heart-knowledge.

'God is greater than our heart, and he knows all things' (meizon estin ho theos tes kardias hemon kai ginoskei panta) states that God is greater than our heart and knows all things. The neuter plural 'all things' (panta, G3956) as object of the present indicative (ongoing, simple statement of fact) 'he knows' (ginoskei, G1097) makes the field of knowing exhaustive (complete) with no temporal qualifier (no limit in time).

'No creature is hidden from his sight, but all are naked and exposed to the eyes of him' (ouk estin ktisis aphanes enopion autou panta de gymna kai tetrachelismena tois ophthalmois autou) denies any creature is hidden 'before him' (enopion, G1799) and declares all things bare and exposed to his eyes. 'Hidden' (aphanes, G0852) is a queried hapax (a word that occurs only once in the entire Bible, here one canon occurrence), and the perfect passive pair (a Greek form for a completed past action whose result still stands, in the form where the subject is acted upon) 'naked' (gymna) and 'exposed' (tetrachelismena) secures both the totality and the durative (ongoing, lasting) state of exposure.

'Truly I say to you, this night, before the rooster crows, you will deny me three times' (amen lego soi hoti en taute te nykti prin alektora phonesai tris aparnese me) records a future free human act predicted in advance with numeric precision (three times) and a timing marker (before the rooster crows). The lexical force is foreknowledge of a future free choice down to count and timing.

'By the determined plan and foreknowledge of God' (te horismene boule kai prognosei tou theou) couples the definite plan of God with his prior knowledge. The dative (a noun in the 'by-X' or 'to-X' grammatical form) 'foreknowledge' (prognosei, G4268) conjoined with 'plan' (boule, G1012) grounds the free human action of lawless executioners ('lawless ones,' anomos, G0459) in a prior divine knowing, so a future free act is held as foreknown.

'Having been predestined according to the purpose of him who works all things according to the counsel of his will' (prooristhentes kata prothesin tou ta panta energountos kata ten boulen tou thelematos autou) places predetermination in line with the one who works all things ('all things,' ta panta, G3956) according to the counsel of his will. The genitive (a noun in the possessive or 'of-X' grammatical form) present participle (ongoing-action form) 'working' (energountos, G1754) with 'all things' (ta panta) asserts exhaustive (complete) providential operation (God's continual sustaining and directing of all things) rooted in prior counsel.

'Those whom he foreknew, he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son' (hous proegno kai proorisen symmorphous tes eikonos tou huiou autou) couples prior knowing ('to know beforehand,' proginosko, G4267) and prior determining ('to determine beforehand,' proorizo, G4309) of those conformed to the Son. The aorist (a completed past action) active pair presents the divine prior cognition as a completed perspective from God's vantage.

'Those whom he predestined, these he also called, and those whom he called, these he also justified, and those whom he justified, these he also glorified' (hous de proorisen toutous kai ekalesen kai edikaiosen kai edoxasen) chains four aorist actives (four completed-past-action verbs in the active voice). The aorist 'he glorified' (edoxasen) places future glorification in the same completed-aspect frame as the prior verbs, consistent with comprehensive divine knowing that views the future as settled.

complicating_texts.resolution: 'Now I know that you fear God' (attah yadati ki yere elohim attah) uses 'to know' (yada, H3045) in the queried qal perfect 1cs form (the simple active completed-action form, first person common singular, tagged HVqp1cs). The same root, the same form, is used of God exhaustively (completely) knowing the heart in 1 Kings 8:39 (qal perfect 2ms, HVqp2ms) and Psalm 139:2 and 139:4, so the verb form is neutral. What shifts the sense is the frame: the unit opens in Genesis 22:1 with 'to test' (nasah, H5254, God tested Abraham), and the identical 'to test' (nasah) plus 'to know' (yada) pairing recurs in Deuteronomy 8:2 (both H5254 and H3045 in one verse, 'to test you and to know what was in your heart'). In a testing frame 'to know' (yada) denotes acknowledgment by demonstration, knowledge made manifest, not cognitive acquisition (gaining new knowledge in the mind). The lexical pattern resolves the verse as forensic disclosure (a public, evidence-style revealing, the kind of showing-forth that happens in a courtroom).

'I will go down now and see' (eredah na ve-ereh) uses 'to see' (raah, H7200, let me see) and then 'to know' (yada, H3045) in the queried qal imperfect cohortative 1cs form (the simple active future-or-volitional form with the 'let me' force, first person common singular, tagged HVqi1cs, 'let me know,' edaah). This is descent-and-investigation language inside a theophanic (a passage in which God appears in visible form) narrative, the speech of judicial action rather than a report of prior ignorance. Read with the pan-canonical (spread across the whole Bible) 'to know' (yada) pattern (1 Kings 8:39, Psalm 94:11, Psalm 139) the cohortative is the idiom of a judge coming to act, not deprivation of knowledge. The vocabulary supplies a juridical-investigation (court-style fact-finding) sense well attested in covenant-lawsuit contexts (passages in which God speaks as a covenant-judge holding court).

'Which I did not command, nor speak, nor did it come up on my heart' (asher lo tsivviti ve-lo dibbarti ve-lo altah al libbi) states what did not come up on my heart. The queried verb is 'to come up' (alah, H5927, came up) with 'heart' (leb, H3820, heart). The exact idiom 'to come up on the heart' (alah al leb) recurs with the same H5927 in Jeremiah 7:31 and Jeremiah 32:35, both speaking of child sacrifice that God did not command or will. The idiom marks what was not decreed (officially decided as God's purpose) or commanded, engaging volition (will or intention), not bare cognition (just knowing in the mind), so the verse does not deny that God foreknew the act. The lexical parallel across three Jeremiah verses fixes the sense as decretal (about what God decided or willed), not epistemic (about what God knew).

'But concerning that day or that hour, no one knows, not even the angels in heaven, nor the Son, but only the Father' (peri de tes hemeras ekeines oudeis oiden ei me ho pater) uses 'to know' (oida) of the Son not knowing the day. The lexeme (the word as a dictionary entry) predicates a limitation in the Son during the incarnate mission (his time on earth as a man), a knowing relative to the economy (the saving plan as it was carried out in history) of his earthly role, set against the broader canonical (Bible-wide) pattern 'he knows all things' (panta ginoskei, 1 John 3:20) and 'there is no creature hidden' (ouk estin ktisis aphanes, Hebrews 4:13). The vocabulary distinguishes a stated economic limit (a limit tied to his role in the saving plan) on the incarnate Son from the divine attribute of exhaustive (complete) knowing, so it qualifies a role, not the essence (the very nature of God).

variants.note: No anchor verse falls in the ingested ECM apparatus (the critical edition of New Testament textual variants) window (3 John 1:1 to 1:15), so 'not_in_ecm_scope' is true in the bundle. Acts 2:23 carries a known variant on 'hand' (cheiros), immaterial to 'foreknowledge' (prognosei) and 'plan' (boule). Ephesians 1:11 has a Western reading (a textual variant from the Western family of manuscripts) on 'we were chosen as an inheritance' (ekleerothemen), but the 'plan' (boule) and 'will' (thelema) language is stable. None of these alter the lexical force, so the verdict is variant robust (stable against textual variants).

competing_lens_verdicts.verdict: affirms exhaustive divine knowledge including future free human actions, held timelessly
competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Reads 'to know beforehand' (proginosko) and 'to determine beforehand' (proorizo) plus 'declaring the end from the beginning' (maggid mereshit acharit) as a direct lexical assertion of exhaustive (complete), settled knowing. The now-I-know and let-me-see texts are taken as accommodated narrative idiom (figures of speech in which God's actions are described in human terms to suit the reader's understanding), specifically forensic 'to know' (yada, knowing-by-demonstration) in a 'testing' (nasah) frame, consistent with 'there is not a word on my tongue' (eyn millah bilshoni) and 'he knows all things' (ginoskei panta).

competing_lens_verdicts.verdict: affirms exhaustive foreknowledge, including counterfactuals of creaturely freedom
competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Coordinates 'foreknowledge' (prognosis, Acts 2:23) and 'plan' (boule) with a knowledge of how free creatures would freely act. The same lexical data (foreknown free act of the executioners, predicted free denial of Peter) is read as middle knowledge (a Molinist category for God's knowledge of what free creatures would do in any situation) that preserves libertarian freedom (the view that a free choice could have gone either way). The words assert that the free acts are foreknown without specifying the mode.

competing_lens_verdicts.verdict: denies exhaustive definite foreknowledge of future free actions, affirms knowledge of all settled reality
competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Takes the now-I-know of Genesis 22:12 and the let-me-see of Genesis 18:21 as real divine learning, and reads 'it did not come up on my heart' (alah al leb) in Jeremiah 19:5 against fixed foreknowledge of the contingent (events that could go more than one way). On this lens the future free act is genuinely open, so God knows it as possibility, not as settled fact. The lexical counterweight is that 'to know' (yada) in Genesis 22:12 is the same qal perfect (simple active completed-action) form used of exhaustive (complete) heart-knowing in 1 Kings 8:39, the testing frame ('to test,' nasah, Deuteronomy 8:2) reads 'to know' (yada) as demonstration, and the Jeremiah 19:5 idiom recurs decretally (in the sense of what God decided or willed) in Jeremiah 7:31 and 32:35.

hermeneutics.notes: Pan-canonical (spread across the whole Bible) density on 'to know' (yada), 'he knows all things' (ginoskei panta), 'to know beforehand' (proginosko), 'to determine beforehand' (proorizo), 'there is not a word on my tongue' (eyn millah), 'there is no searching' (eyn cheqer), and the 'declaring the end from the beginning' (maggid mereshit acharit) declaration favors exhaustive (complete) knowing across both Testaments. The divergence among lenses turns on whether the anthropomorphic (described in human terms) knowing and testing idioms are accommodated narrative speech (figures used to suit the reader, not literal limits in God) or ontologically binding limits (real limits in God's very being), and on whether future free acts are foreknown as settled or as open possibility. Each lens is stated in its strongest lexical form, and the verdict is not assigned to any tradition.

stem_audit.notes: The stem states that God knows all things (actual and possible, past, present, future) exhaustively (completely) and eternally, including all future free human actions. This is descriptive of the claim under test, not loaded toward one tradition, since the future-free-actions clause is precisely the contested scope that open theism disputes. The lexicon was queried to test whether the canon language carries exhaustive (complete) knowing and whether the now-I-know and let-me-see idioms qualify it. The prior file verdict of 'affirms true' is retained on real queried evidence.

lay_summary: Across both Testaments the words point clearly to God knowing all things completely and eternally. In Psalm 139 the verb 'to know' (yada, Strong H3045, queried at 945 occurrences in the Hebrew text) is used for God searching the writer, knowing his sitting and rising, his ways, and a word before it reaches the tongue. The phrase 'there is not a word on my tongue' (eyn millah bilshoni) declares there is no word in the mouth that God does not already know. Isaiah 40:28 adds 'there is no searching out of his understanding' (eyn cheqer), and Isaiah 46:10 has 'declaring the end from the beginning' (maggid mereshit acharit). The New Testament continues the pattern. First John 3:20 puts 'he knows all things' (ginoskei panta) with God as subject, the object made total. Hebrews 4:13 stacks the negation 'there is no creature hidden' (ouk estin ktisis aphanes) with the perfect participles 'naked' (gymna) and 'exposed' (tetrachelismena), all things bare and laid open to his eyes. Matthew 26:34 has Jesus predict Peter denying him three times before the rooster crows, and Acts 2:23 binds 'foreknowledge' (prognosis) with the divine plan, so future free human acts are spoken of as foreknown. The recurring terms and their spread across narrative, wisdom, prophecy, gospel, and letter make the pattern decisive. Where readers diverge is on a small set of texts that sound like God learning. Genesis 22:12 says 'now I know that you fear God' (yada), but the verb there is the very same form of 'to know' (yada) used in 1 Kings 8:39 for God alone knowing every heart, and the chapter opens by saying God 'tested' (nasah) Abraham, the same testing-plus-knowing pairing found in Deuteronomy 8:2, so the words read as knowledge shown by a test rather than knowledge gained. Genesis 18:21 has God descend to see, the speech of a judge coming to act. Jeremiah 19:5 says 'it did not come up on my heart' (alah al leb), but the same idiom in Jeremiah 7:31 and 32:35 means God did not command or will it. So the divergence is genuinely lexical (a matter of the actual word patterns). It hangs on whether these knowing and testing idioms are figures suited to the reader or real limits, and on whether a future free choice is known as settled fact or open possibility. The wider word pattern weighs toward accommodated idiom and settled knowing.
